content: In 2007, the UNAIDS report indicated that approximately 7 million individuals in India were living with HIV. However, this number has since been revised to an estimated range of 2 to 3 million. This adjustment places India's HIV prevalence rate below that of several Western nations, including the United States, Canada, Italy, France, and Spain, at 0.36%. India's HIV epidemic is not uniform but rather consists of multiple localized epidemics, some of which occur within the same state. The modes of transmission vary significantly across regions. In many states, heterosexual transmission accounts for approximately 85% of cases, often linked to interactions with commercial sex workers. In contrast, in certain other states, intravenous drug use is the predominant route of HIV transmission. Monitoring the epidemic and implementing effective intervention programs remain significant challenges for Indian authorities and communities. HIV surveillance in India is overseen by the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO). Most of the surveillance data collected by NACO is derived from annual unlinked anonymous testing of individuals attending prenatal (antenatal) clinics and sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics. These annual surveillance reports are publicly accessible on NACO's official website. India faces unique challenges in addressing HIV/AIDS due to its large population, high population density, low literacy rates, and consequently low levels of awareness about the disease. HIV/AIDS continues to be one of the most formidable public health issues the country has ever encountered. A study published in the British medical journal The Lancet in 2006 reported a significant decline of approximately 30% in HIV infections among young women aged 15 to 24 who attended prenatal clinics in selected southern states of India between 2000 and 2004. These regions are considered to have concentrated epidemics. The authors of the study cautiously attributed this decline to increased condom use among men who engage with commercial sex workers. They also cited multiple pieces of corroborating evidence to support this conclusion.
